Summary:

The manuscript by Hernández-Rocamora et al. describes a FRET-based real time assay that allows for continuous monitoring of peptidoglycan synthesis by aPBPs. The authors examine how the assay performs in detergent and in liposomes; they also assess whether the assay will be useful for studying regulators of peptidoglycan biosynthesis enzymes by applying it to previously studied lipoprotein activators of aPBPs, and a new lipoprotein activator that is similar to a previously studied one. The major advantage of the current assay in comparison to the original dansylated lipid II assay is that the FRET assay can monitor both GTase and TPase activities. Finally, the current FRET assay has the potential to become single-molecule study-compatible. The Vollmer lab is one of only a few that can carry out studies of PG biosynthetic enzymes, and he has teamed up with an expert in microscopy on this manuscript. The experiments are technically challenging and generally well done and the technical advances should be useful to the field. However, new biological/mechanistic insights are few. The work also needs to be significantly strengthened with more critically analyzed data, control experiments and better writing.

Reviewer #1:

1) FRET controls and calculations:

a) The authors should provide donor-only and acceptor-only controls under the same conditions for all experiments to allow the calculation of FRET efficiency quantitatively (preferably using the Ratio A method Clegg RM, Methods in Enzymology, 1992, 211, p353). This quantification is important because one major potential advantage of this method could be studying the kinetics of GTase and TPase activities, which may offer mechanistic insight on the enzyme's working. The Facceptor /Fdonor ratio measurement is convenient and can be useful for screening of a large sample size but is prone to artifacts such as fluorescence quenching due to reasons other than FRET, especially when the way the system is set up does not allow precise determination of the donor/acceptor ratio and attachment positions. These donor only or acceptor only experiments are also important for the FRAP measurement in the SLB assay.

b) In Figure 4 the authors used a ratiometric FRET equation Erel = IA/(IA+ID) in the semi-single-molecule assay to determine FRET efficiency. This measurement should be unified to allow direct comparison of FRET between different types of experiments (solubilized, liposomes, SLBs, bulk or single-molecule). As mentioned above, the acceptor intensity consists of the intensities from donor-excitation (FRET), direct-excitation, and bleed-through from the donor. Donor emission could be quenched due to reasons (such as the local environment as that in the dansyl-lipid II assay) other than FRET. More control experiments will allow the authors to determine how this impact the true acceptor signal resulting from FRET.

c) There appears to be a major difference in the fluorescence intensity spectra between the detergent-solubilized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and liposome experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, C, D). In the detergent solubilized experiments, there appears to be little change in the intensity of the donor peak from PBP1B to +LpoB. However, in the liposome experiments the LpoB has a drastic loss of donor signal compared to that of PBP1B. This is another reason why calculating FRET efficiency instead of the relative ratio would allow for a better comparison between the experiments. This drastic loss of donor signal in the liposome experiments is seen in all 3 species. The authors should address why there is such a difference in the FRET profiles between these two experiments.

d) The authors rely on "Relative Slope" to show how the addition of LpoB impacts the PBP1B activity. Is the "Relative slope" calculated by normalizing the slope of a reaction with LopB to that without LopB? How is the time window determined? As this ratio does not really inform on the enzyme activity, it would be difficult for other groups to use the same method and to compare to this metric. It is also difficult to judge whether the GTase is faster or slower in the presence of TPase activity without the absolute values. Please provide the absolute measurement of the slope (or the initial velocity V0) using a better determined FRET efficiency value as in point 1a.

e) Additionally, perhaps the authors could determine the reaction velocities at different substrate concentrations to see if Michaelis-Menten kinetics could be applied? A reanalysis of the data with better quantifications with regard to enzyme's kinetics would benefit the community significantly by providing a more complete picture of enzyme's activity rather than only comparing PBP1B alone to +LpoB.

2) According to the authors' data and others' work, PBP1B can only synthesize short, uncrosslinked PG chains when its TPase is inhibited. When the TPase is not inhibited, the crosslinking could somehow help and accelerate the PG chains synthesis by the GTase. The entire signal change should be because of both GTase and TPase activities. The authors mentioned that the first slow phase reflects the GTase activity and the second fast phase reflects the TPase, but I do not find it convincing.

a) Please define which section is slow and which section is fast in the FRET curves-in the presence of LpoB, it does not appear to have a slow-phase if the initial lag phase of rise is the slow-phase the authors mentioned.

b) In the presence of Amp, the slope of the initial rise appears to be slower than that in the absence of Amp, which, could be the reason that the authors argue that TPase help accelerate GTase. Please provide absolute quantifications using FRET efficiency to show that this is indeed the case.

c) Can the authors add D,D-endopeptidase in the system after the end of the reaction to uncrosslink the peptides and see how much FRET signal remains, which should be contributed by the pure GTase activity? This signal could be compared with that in the presence of Amp to examine the authors' claim.

3) The lag of TPase activity behind GTase activity as shown in Figure 1F is intriguing. The lag appears to be on the order of 5-10 min in this system and suggest that the GTase and TPase activities are not synchronous. Does this mean that even though PBP1B has both activities in one single molecule, but the two reactions are catalyzed asynchronously by two different molecules?

4) The authors suggest that the decrease of FRET signal in Figure 2C, E and G is due to additional changes of fluorophore's spectroscopic properties. If so why such changes were not observed in the detergent or SLB experiments, if the product is the same? The authors should obtain parallel time points using radio-labeled Lipid II and run the products of both assays on HPLC to show that the decrease of FRET signal in these experiments did not correspond to changed product.

5) The SLB assay has great potentials to allow single-molecule measurement of glycan chain elongation and crosslinking kinetics. It is disappointing, though, to find out that no single-lipid II molecules in the polymerized PG can be visualized. Is this because the lipid II concentration too high on the SLB? Does it need to be that high?

6) To fully drive home the message that the new FRET is better in many ways than previous assays, the authors should compare it with the dansyl-lipid II assay side by side (i.e., not putting the other assay in the supplemental figures) and quantitatively.

7) Similarly, there appeared to be significant differences in FRET signals between the detergent, liposome and SLB assays with or without Amp, and it is difficult to compare the enhancement by LpoB among these assays. Please address these differences.

Reviewer #2:

1) It is stated that: "As expected, ampicillin did not prevent the stimulation of PBP1B by LpoB(sol), which accelerated the FRET increase by 10-20 times with or without ampicillin, consistent with the previously reported stimulation of both GTase and TPase activities." Although other results may suggest TPase activity is stimulated, one cannot draw the conclusion from the FRET assay results here that LpoB stimulates TPase activity – only that TPase activity boosts the FRET signal. There is some confusion in the manuscript about what can and cannot be concluded about mechanism from the FRET assays.

2) The authors use initial rates from the FRET assay to compare effects of LpoB in Figure 1 (and later do the same for other conditions/other activators). Initial rate conditions are used to quantify reaction rates for enzymes because under these conditions substrate depletion and product inhibition do not impact the rate. Initial rates are misleading when comparing a hyperbolic progress curve to a sigmoidal progress curve. The authors should comment on this, clarify the time frame over which the initial rates were measured (perhaps indicated with a figure), and also report the slopes of the "fast" phase of the reactions where activator is not present.

3) There is a pattern of low mass bands in the PAGE gel in Figure 1D for the LpoB reactions; these are barely visible in the reactions without LpoB. At the same time, the glycan strands are shorter in length for the LpoB reaction compared to the reaction without LpoB (lanes 2 and 6). (Shorter glycan strands were observed previously for LpoB - e.g, Paradis-Bleau et al.; Lupoli et al.). I am curious about whether these observations are connected (and therefore whether they are connected to how LpoB achieves activation).

4) The authors comment that the combined assays suggest that the total FRET signal emerges from two steps that have different rates. I recommend either refining or removing this comment. The statement suggests that it might be possible to extract rates for the two steps alluded to from the FRET signal. But there are more than two steps and two rates. For polymerization reactions, initiation and elongation rates are often substantially different and there is evidence in the literature that this is case for PG synthesis. (The slow rate of reaction for the "only labelled Lipid II" reactions does not report on the rate of polymerization with unlabeled Lipid II present because the products are very short – so the polymerization does not "take off" the way it does in the other reactions.) Moreover, there are likely two rates for crosslinking in vitro because the first crosslinks are formed intermolecularly and later crosslinks are formed intramolecularly. Finally, the FRET signal itself is different for uncrosslinked and crosslinked PG – as the authors note, it reaches a higher maximum for the latter.

5) Figure 2C: was the lane 7 sample in the gel the same as the one for which the fluorescence trace is shown? The fluorescence trace looks flat but lane 7 shows polymerization. In other gels, other lanes that show comparable levels of polymerization also show a FRET signal.

6) I already mentioned that the discussion could use some work, but wanted to elaborate. The explanation for how TPase activity increases the FRET signal is plausible and supported by the data. But the section on "coupled reactions in Class A PBPs" is confusing because it is not clear what the authors are trying to accomplish with it. There has been a lot of debate about what LpoB does to activate PBP1b and how it does it. That LpoB affects both GTase activity and TPase activity has been shown repeatedly to one degree or another, and the idea that one activity influences the other in this context has been discussed explicitly going back at least to 2014 (Egan et al., 2014; Lupoli et al., 2014). The authors discuss the idea again here, evidently in response to a recent paper (Catherwood et al.) that attributes LpoB's essentiality to its effects on TPase activity. They conclude that Catherwood's conditions may have overemphasized the TPase effect. I don't think arguing this point is the most important use of the discussion space. The authors should clarify how they think about what the FRET assays show with respect to mechanism of Lpo activators and try to connect their work to a path forward.

Summary: there is a lot of nice material in this manuscript and I believe the authors are pushing the field ahead with the FRET assays, particularly their use in SLMs. However, the analysis of the results is not at the same level as the technical innovations and this should be improved. Mainly text revisions could make the paper suitable for eLife, but it will take some work on the part of the authors.

Reviewer #3:

This manuscript describes studies of generation of improved in vitro assay systems for peptidoglycan synthesis, using liposomes and supported lipid bilayers. This work can be very influential as this synthetic process is a primer candidate for the development for additional antibiotics, and the detection methods utilized are potentially adaptable to high-throughput screens.

Overall the paper is well written and the data are convincing. I have a few comments below, primarily concerning the data presentation.

1) Figures 1A, 2B, and 5: These figures show some of the fluorescently-labeled peptides as being involved in crosslinks. I do not think there is evidence in this paper that these substrates are ever used by transpeptidases. They do not appear to show up in obvious radioactively-labeled HPLC peaks. Doesn't this suggest that they are NOT being crosslinked? All off the crosslinked material seen in HPLC peaks is simply the radiolabeled Lipid II.

2) Figure 1C: I don't understand why the slope with LpoB is greater in the presence of Amp? Can the authors comment?

Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Olga Boudker as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

As the editors have judged that your manuscript is of interest, but as described below that additional experiments are still required before it is published. We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). First, because many researchers have temporarily lost access to the labs, we will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts. We are also offering, if you choose, to post the manuscript to bioRxiv (if it is not already there) along with this decision letter and a formal designation that the manuscript is "in revision at eLife". Please let us know if you would like to pursue this option. (If your work is more suitable for medRxiv, you will need to post the preprint yourself, as the mechanisms for us to do so are still in development.)

Major comments:

The major advantages of the assay are three-fold, (1) it is a real-time; (2) it is applicable to membrane-embedded enzymes, and (3) it can monitor both GTase and TPase. The revised manuscript has provided evidence for all the three with improved clarity, new control experiments, and better FRET efficiency calculations, but it still lacks the rigor in the quantitative (or semi-quantitative) aspect of the assay. Specifically, the authors need to provide evidence that the Facceptor/Fdonor ratio indeed reflects proportionally to either just the GTase activity or a combined GTase and TPase activity. The authors did show qualitatively that this ratio is altered when the activator LpoB (or P) or drugs are used, but it is difficult to use this ratio to compare quantitatively (or semi-quantitatively) the rates of different reactions catalyzed by different enzymes, or the same enzyme but with different mutations and regulators. Being able to do so will greatly enhance the impact of the FRET assay and promote its wide adoption in the field.

It appears that the measured Facceptor/Fdonor ratio is not only dependent on the GTase and TPase activities of PBP1B, but some other effects that influence the fluorescence of the dyes. These other effects will make it difficult to use the FRET assay to quantitatively compare different reactions. For example, in Figure 3C, the reaction with Amp (VII) barely had any signal change in Facceptor/Fdonor, but the corresponding gel lane cleared showed polymerized, linear PG strands, suggesting that the polymerization reaction is not reflected in the fluorescence ratio measurement. The rise and decay of the +LpoB/Amp (III) reaction also look strange-this reaction had a similar PG ladder on the gel as reaction (-LpoB/Amp)VII, but the fluorescence ratio measurements are drastically different. Another example is the comparison between the three PBP1Bs: it appears that crosslinking activities have different contributions to the fluorescence ratio measurement: ampicillin completely abolished the fluorescence ratio signal for PBP1BEc but not for PBP1BAb. It is hard to imagine that these highly homologous enzymes would have very different mechanisms to synthesize PG.

A likely explanation for these different fluorescence signals in these reactions is probably what the authors suggested, that some spectroscopic properties of the dyes changed due to the incorporation and/or local environment. Another possibility is that these enzymes of different species may handle the dye-labeled LipidII differentially, one PBP1B may have more difficulty in accepting the dye-labeled LipidII than the other PBP1B. Yet another possibility could also be that the stimulation effect of LpoB is simply that now more dye-labeled LipidII v.s. unlabeled Lipid II can be incorporated, but not necessarily the rate at which Lipid II is incorporated.

It is understandable that these in vitro experiments are extremely challenging, but fluorescence measurements are sensitive and prone to artifacts, and the authors should perform control experiments to make sure that the measured signal indeed reflects the desired enzymatic activities. In particular, in calculating the fluorescence ratio, the donor-only and acceptor-only controls need to be run simultaneously to determine how much fluorescence change is due to the local environment change, and how much is due to FRET. The authors have performed these control experiments but only used them for the end-point measurements. These controls should also be performed for the real-time measurements (with LpoB, with or without Amp), which could help to explain some strange changes in the measured fluorescence ratio (such as that in Figure 3C).

The goal, hopefully, is that one can confidently interpret the ~ 25-fold higher initial slope of PBP1BEc with LpoB in the presence of ampicillin as a 25-fold (or proportionally) higher GTase activity of PBP1BEc stimulated by LpoB (such as that in Figure 3D). Similarly, one can use the smaller fold-increase of the initial slopes in the cases of PBP1BAb and PBP1BPa in the presence of their cognate activators to draw the conclusion that these activators do not stimulate these PBP1Bs to the same extent as that of PBP1BEc. If the fold enhancement of the initial slopes by LpoB in the presence and absence of ampicillin are similar to each other, one perhaps can say that here LpoB only stimulates the GTase activity, and so on and so forth.

The new FRET assay bears great potential in providing a sensitive and quantitative way to characterize both GTase and TPase activities in ways not possible before. The Vollmer laboratory also has the expertise to make this assay hugely impactful for the field. These experiments can become powerful, but they need critical controls.

results.result: A novel FRET-based assay was developed to monitor in real time both GTase and TPase reactions of class A PBPs reconstituted in liposomes or supported lipid bilayers. The assay was successfully applied to PBP1B homologues from E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and A. baumannii in the presence or absence of their cognate lipoprotein activators.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C5 describe the main methodological contribution of the manuscript. The development and application of the FRET assay is extensively supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript (Figures 1-5 and supplementary figures), demonstrating its functionality across multiple bacterial species and conditions.

results.result: Fluorescently labeled lipid II (Atto550 and Atto647n) is incorporated into PG by PBP1BEc, resulting in FRET that depends on both GTase and TPase activity, with TPase being the major contributor. FRET efficiency was 29±6%, which was reduced to one-third by ampicillin (TPase inhibitor) and abolished by moenomycin (GTase inhibitor).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1B-D showing incorporation of both fluorescent probes, FRET signal generation, and differential effects of specific inhibitors. The quantitative FRET efficiency measurements and the clear demonstration of antibiotic effects provide strong evidence for the conclusion that TPase is the major contributor to FRET.

results.result: Real-time monitoring of PBP1BEc activity in detergents showed that without LpoB, FRET appeared after ~5 min and plateaued after 50-60 min, while with LpoB(sol), FRET increased immediately and plateaued after 10-20 min. LpoB increased reaction slopes approximately 10- or 20-fold in the absence or presence of ampicillin, respectively. Moenomycin abolished FRET, while ampicillin reduced it threefold.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 and C41 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1E-F showing real-time FRET curves and quantified slopes. The data clearly demonstrate the activating effect of LpoB and the differential effects of antibiotics, with appropriate controls and quantification.

results.result: Digestion experiments with MepM (endopeptidase) and cellosyl (muramidase) demonstrated that inter-chain FRET is a major contributor to the total FRET signal. MepM reduced FRET efficiency by approximately twofold for crosslinked PG but had negligible effect on glycan chains produced with ampicillin. Cellosyl completely abolished FRET for both products. FRET correlated with formation of crosslinked muropeptide dimers, not lipid II consumption rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-E showing the effects of enzymatic digestion on FRET and correlation with HPLC analysis of products. The differential effects of MepM (which cleaves crosslinks) versus cellosyl (which cleaves glycan chains) provide strong evidence for the conclusion that inter-chain FRET dominates the signal.

results.result: PBP1BEc alone could not polymerize fluorescently labeled lipid II without unlabeled lipid II, but addition of LpoB enabled production of short, non-crosslinked chains with slow but large FRET increase. Experiments varying the proportion of fluorescent lipid II showed that LpoB stimulates incorporation of fluorophores in consecutive positions along glycan chains, increasing intra-chain FRET contribution. The increase in reaction slopes with activator reflects both higher PG synthesis rate and higher intra-chain FRET contribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C60 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, showing the requirement for unlabeled lipid II, the effect of LpoB on polymerization of labeled substrates, and systematic variation of fluorescent lipid II proportions. The data provide strong evidence for the conclusion about LpoB's effect on intra-chain FRET, though the interpretation involves some inference about the mechanism.

results.result: PBP1BEc was successfully reconstituted in liposomes with the N-terminus inside, as demonstrated by accessibility assays. The liposome-reconstituted enzyme required absence of NaCl for improved activity and showed slower reaction rates than detergent-solubilized enzyme, with longer lag times. LpoB(sol) produced approximately tenfold increase in initial slope and much higher final FRET. Both fluorescent probes were incorporated into PG products in liposomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C72 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-C and supplementary figures showing protein orientation, activity requirements, and FRET measurements in liposomes. The data demonstrate successful reconstitution and functional activity, though the slower rates in liposomes compared to detergents suggest some limitations of the system.

results.result: A hypothetical lipoprotein (LpoPAb) containing two tetratricopeptide repeats was identified next to the PBP1BAb gene and found to activate PBP1BAb. LpoPAb(sol) stimulated PBP1BAb GTase activity ~3.3-fold and accelerated lipid II consumption and glycan chain polymerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 are supported by bioinformatic analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 6) showing identification and functional characterization of LpoPAb. The discovery of a novel activator for A. baumannii PBP1B is well-supported by the data.

results.result: PBP1BAb showed low FRET signal and poor crosslinked PG production in detergents, but displayed higher TPase activity in liposomes with substantially higher final FRET signal. Ampicillin had negligible effect in detergents and only small effect in liposomes (~1.2-fold reduction), indicating intra-chain FRET is the major contributor. LpoPAb(sol) stimulated PBP1BAb more strongly in detergents (12.3-fold) than liposomes (~2.5-fold).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3E-F and supplementary figures showing differential activity of PBP1BAb in detergents versus liposomes. The data demonstrate that membrane environment significantly affects enzyme activity, with important implications for understanding physiological function.

results.result: PBP1BPa displayed robust TPase activity in both detergents and liposomes. Ampicillin reduced final FRET by ~1.8-fold in detergents and ~1.5-fold in liposomes, indicating substantial inter-chain FRET contribution. LpoPPa(sol) increased final FRET ~2-fold and accelerated initial slopes ~4-11-fold, with increased lipid II consumption under both conditions, indicating stimulation of both GTase and TPase activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3G-H and supplementary figures showing PBP1BPa activity in different environments and the effects of LpoPPa. The data are consistent with a recent report (Caveney et al., 2020) and demonstrate that the FRET assay can detect dual activation of both enzymatic activities.

results.result: Single PBP1BEc molecules reconstituted in supported lipid bilayers could be tracked by TIRF microscopy. PBP1BEc diffused with average Dcoef of 0.23±0.06 µm²/s, which decreased to 0.10±0.06 µm²/s upon addition of lipid II. Prolonged confined motion was not detected, but average displacement length between frames was reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4B-E and Video 1 showing single-molecule tracking of fluorescently labeled PBP1BEc. The data demonstrate successful reconstitution at low density and provide quantitative measurements of diffusion changes upon substrate addition, supporting the interpretation that substrate binding slows enzyme diffusion.

results.result: SLB-reconstituted PBP1BEc incorporated about 12% of added radiolabeled lipid II into PG after overnight incubation with LpoB(sol). HPLC analysis revealed production of both GTase and TPase products that were absent with moenomycin. About 32% of radioactivity remained in membrane fraction after washing, with no PG products in wash fraction, confirming PG synthesis occurred on SLBs and remained attached. PBP1BEc did not affect lipid II binding to bilayer.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C103 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing radioactive lipid II incorporation and HPLC analysis of products. The data demonstrate that PBP1BEc remains active on SLBs and produces membrane-attached PG, though the low incorporation efficiency (12%) suggests limitations of the system at very low enzyme density.

results.result: FRET was detected on SLBs by acceptor photobleaching after addition of unlabeled lipid II and LpoB(sol), with signal increasing after ~8 min lag phase. No FRET increase occurred with ampicillin, GTase-defective PBP1BEc (E233Q), or after cellosyl digestion, indicating the FRET signal is primarily due to transpeptidase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-C and supplementary figures showing FRET detection by microscopy with appropriate controls. The multiple lines of evidence (ampicillin inhibition, GTase mutant, cellosyl digestion) strongly support the conclusion that TPase activity is the primary contributor to FRET on SLBs.

results.result: During PG synthesis on SLBs, the diffusion coefficient of lipid II-Atto647n decreased 2-3-fold in a time-dependent manner when crosslinking was permitted (no ampicillin), reaching minimum at ~10 min similar to FRET lag. The immobile fraction did not change significantly (13±2% vs 18±6% with/without ampicillin, p=0.15). Ampicillin only affected lipid II diffusivity (2.9±0.4 vs 0.67±0.1 µm²/s), not membrane lipid probe diffusivity (1.6±0.65 vs 1.94±0.62 µm²/s), indicating lipid II was incorporated into small groups of crosslinked glycan chains that remain mobile.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C117 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5B-F showing FRAP analysis of lipid II and membrane probe diffusion during PG synthesis. The data provide strong evidence that crosslinked PG remains mobile on SLBs but diffuses more slowly, with appropriate controls demonstrating membrane fluidity is not affected by the synthesis reaction.

results.result: For all PBPs tested, FRET increased with GTase activity alone (intra-chain FRET) but was always higher with active TPase (inter-chain FRET). For PBP1BEc, FRET curves closely followed crosslinked PG production rate and decreased substantially upon endopeptidase digestion, indicating inter-chain FRET is a main component. The authors hypothesize that TPase brings glycan chains into close proximity, reducing probe distances to produce high FRET, possibly because steric constraints prevent incorporation of two large fluorescent lipid II molecules at successive positions in a single chain.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122, C124-C125 summarize key findings about FRET mechanisms supported by data in Figures 1-3 and supplementary figures. The conclusion that inter-chain FRET dominates is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence (antibiotic effects, enzymatic digestion, HPLC correlation). The hypothesis about steric constraints (C122) is speculative but reasonable given the data and prior work (Van't Veer et al., 2016).

results.result: The overall FRET signal combines intra-chain and inter-chain FRET, which depend on average distances and orientation of fluorophores on growing glycan chains. There is currently no method to measure these parameters individually, preventing determination of absolute GTase and TPase rates. Different PBPs may produce different fluorophore distributions, and activators can enhance incorporation of fluorescent lipid II analogues. The assay is inherently semi-quantitative, but with appropriate controls it can determine whether FRET follows more the GTase or TPase reaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C130 accurately describe the limitations of the FRET assay. These are honest assessments supported by the experimental observations (e.g., C129 is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The authors appropriately acknowledge that the assay is semi-quantitative while demonstrating its utility for comparative studies.

results.result: All three PBP1B homologues (E. coli, P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii) started reactions after a lag phase that was abolished by cognate activators. The authors suggest this slow start and its acceleration by Lpo activators could be an important mechanism to initiate PG synthesis at gaps in the PG layer where activators can contact the synthase.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work showing the lag phase and activator effects. Claim C133 is speculative but reasonable given recent work on PBP1B's role in cell wall repair (Vigouroux et al., 2020; Morè et al., 2019). The speculation is appropriately presented as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.

results.result: The authors critique a recent report (Catherwood et al., 2020) that concluded LpoB-mediated TPase activation explains LpoB essentiality, noting that assay used enzyme concentrations too low to support GTase activity without LpoB. They propose an alternative explanation: LpoB essentiality is explained by >10-fold GTase stimulation, and activation by LpoB was much more needed when PBP1B was membrane-embedded compared to detergent-solubilized. In vitro, LpoB also stimulated TPase, producing hyper-crosslinked PG, as observed for LpoPPa and PBP1BPa.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C140 present a critique of prior work and alternative interpretation supported by the current data and citations. The critique (C136) is valid and supported by prior work (Pazos et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2007). The alternative explanation (C137-C138) is well-supported by the experimental data showing stronger LpoB requirement in membrane environments. Claims C139-C140 are supported by citations to prior work.

results.result: Slower reaction rates were found in liposomes than detergents for all enzymes tested. Several factors could explain this (slow lipid II incorporation, limited liposome capacity, undecaprenyl pyrophosphate accumulation), but none should change with LpoB. The authors favor the explanation that membrane-embedding of PBP1B hinders lipid II binding, slowing the reaction.
results.evaluation: Claim C143 is supported by experimental data comparing detergent and liposome conditions. Claims C144-C146 present possible explanations, with C144 supported by citation to prior work on undecaprenyl pyrophosphate inhibition. The preferred explanation (C146) is speculative but reasonable given the data, particularly the observation that LpoB effects differ between environments.

results.result: PBP1BAb showed higher TPase activity in liposomes than detergents, highlighting that detergents can affect membrane protein activity and that experimental conditions in PG synthesis assays should be as close as possible to physiological conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C148 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3E and supplementary figures showing differential activity of PBP1BAb in different environments. This observation reinforces the importance of the membrane-reconstituted assay system and is an important finding for the field.

results.result: FRET signal increase was detected on SLBs upon triggering PG synthesis, correlating with transpeptidation. Diffusion of reaction products could be followed, indicating PBP1BEc produced smaller patches of crosslinked glycan chains rather than completely covering surfaces with PG. This is attributed to very low PBP1BEc density required to ensure SLB homogeneity and stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C151 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing FRET detection and product diffusion on SLBs. The interpretation that small patches are produced (C150) is reasonable given the low enzyme density (C151) and the observation that products remain mobile. This is an important finding demonstrating the assay's capability for spatial analysis.

results.result: A reduction of PBP1BEc diffusivity was detected in the presence of lipid II. Previous in vivo single-molecule tracking reported two populations (fast diffusing and almost immobile), with the immobile population assumed to be active. The current result supports this interpretation, though more experiments are needed.
results.evaluation: Claim C152 is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing reduced diffusion upon lipid II addition. Claims C153-C154 appropriately connect this finding to prior in vivo work (Cho et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; Vigouroux et al., 2020) while acknowledging the need for further validation. The support for the prior interpretation is reasonable but appropriately cautious.

results.result: Important advantages of the new assay include use of natural transpeptidation substrates (nascent glycan strands) instead of pentapeptide mimics, and ability to measure activities in natural lipid environment. The assay can potentially be adopted to study PG synthases with interacting proteins (monofunctional PBPs with GTases, interacting class A PBPs) and for high-throughput screening for new antimicrobials.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C159 accurately describe advantages of the assay that are demonstrated by the experimental data. Claims C160-C161 are speculative about future applications but reasonable given the demonstrated capabilities of the assay. The speculation is appropriately presented as potential rather than established capability.

results.result: Background claims about peptidoglycan structure and function: PG is an essential component of the bacterial cell envelope composed of glycan strands of alternating GlcNAc and MurNAc residues interconnected by short peptides, forming a mesh-like layer that protects cells from osmotic lysis and maintains cell shape. Class A PBPs are bifunctional synthases that polymerize glycan chains and crosslink peptides. Important antibiotics target PG biosynthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C6-C7 present established knowledge about peptidoglycan and class A PBPs, supported by the citation to Vollmer et al., 2008 for C7. These are accurate statements of background knowledge that provide context for the study.

results.result: Background claims about PBP inhibitors, regulation, and lipid II synthesis: Moenomycin inhibits GTase and β-lactams inhibit TPase function of class A PBPs. In E. coli, PBP1A and PBP1B account for substantial PG synthesis activity and are regulated by multiple proteins including LpoA and LpoB. Lipid II can be synthesized chemically, semi-enzymatically, or isolated from cells with inactivated MurJ.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C15 present established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These provide important background for understanding the experimental system and are accurately stated.

results.result: Background claims about limitations of existing PG synthesis assays: Most current assays are end-point assays that don't provide real-time information, involve laborious techniques incompatible with high-throughput screening, or exclusively report on either GTase or TPase but not both. Many include detergents and/or high DMSO concentrations that affect enzyme activity. Detergent-solubilized enzymes have very different environment compared to membrane-confined enzymes.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C26 accurately describe limitations of existing methods, supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims establish the rationale for developing the new FRET assay and are well-supported by the literature.
